Accordingly, from the transformer’s mechanics we derive two properties: (i) clustered locality and among-query continuity of critical indices, and (ii) progressive cross-layer propagation of information. III-A Observation 1: Critical Tokens Exist in Clustered Manners Prior work [ 28 , 12 , 42 ] shows that consecutive decoding queries are close in embedding space and often share critical indices, which motivates KV sharing strategies. However, per-head selections can still vary markedly, and the overlap between selected indices remains small even for high cosine similarity between queries [ 43 ] , leading to suboptimal sharing. For example, HShare [ 42 ] shares indices directly, missing many truly critical indices at high sharing ratios. To bridge this gap, we observe that critical indices organize into a small number of clusters that persist across adjacent queries, providing a more stable sharing unit than individual indices. Property 1 (Among-query Property) . For two semantically similar consecutive queries, the centroids of their critical-token clusters undergo a smooth mean shift along the sequence axis. As shown in Fig. 2 , when the cosine similarity between q t q_{t} and q t + 1 q_{t+1} exceeds 0.8 0.8 , critical indices concentrate into a few clusters; although cluster centers and spreads shift slightly, the cluster-level overlap remains large. Our theoretical analysis further shows that these clusters satisfy a mean-shift (bounded drift) property, formalized in Theorem 1 . Theorem 1 (Centroid Drift) . This smooth drift is consistent with empirical attention patterns and with StreamingLLM’s “keep a few initial tokens” observation [ 45 ] . In summary, across heads and layers, the critical tokens of successive similar queries form dense, localized clusters . We call this the sink effect : tokens near a high-attention location inherit elevated attention due to semantic proximity . Exploring the effect enables explicit control under PrHS, our CIS operationalizes this by dilating shared sets to cover the local cluster and compensate for centroid drift, avoiding full per-head re-retrieval. Detailed proofs are in Appendix A . III-B Observation 2: Information Propagates Progressively Among Layers Locality-bias analyses [ 49 , 6 ] show that attention is sharply concentrated locally within a narrow window around the current query and the sink token, across diverse prompts (Fig. 3 ). This suggests that the current token draws most information from recent tokens, whereas the sink token acts as an attractor rather than conveying semantic content. Viewed in isolation, such constrained receptive fields would only support short-term memory for LLMs, seemingly at odds with their strong long-context performance. Moreover, recent studies [ 2 , 39 , 5 ] show that: across layers, intermediate tokens incrementally absorb the semantics of their relevant predecessors; by higher layers, a mid-sequence token encodes both its own content and a compressed synopsis of earlier, distant tokens. It means that stacking transformer layers realizes long-range dependency paths through chains of neighboring tokens even when no individual layer attends broadly. Consequently, salient long-distance information is distilled into nearby carrier tokens, reducing the marginal importance of many earlier ones; hence, later layers need not re-scan the full prefix. Building on this insight, PSAW and ETF prune KV entries whose instantaneous (per-layer) and accumulated (cross-layer) attention mass fall below preset thresholds, ensuring that the total dropped mass remains within β th \beta_{\mathrm{th}} ; by Eq. ( 4 ), this certifies a bounded MI loss. We formalize these guarantees in Appendix C-D . Fig. 4: Critical-index set (CIS) dilation. IV Proposed Method and Implementation In this section we present CPE. First, CIS (from Observation 1) enables efficient head-level KV sharing across adjacent queries. Next, PSAW and ETF (from Observation 2) prune redundant attention by shrinking visible attention window and freezing early token updates, respectively, with theoretical error guarantees. We also describe CUDA kernels for parallel index manipulation and sparse attention. IV-A Clustered Indices Sharing (CIS) CIS performs head-level KV sharing with dilated shared set among semantically similar, and temporally adjacent queries. By Observation 1 and Theorem 1 , the critical clusters for such queries undergo only small mean shifts relative to a reference query. Therefore, exhaustive per-query head-level retrieval is unnecessary. We first partition the sequence into fixed-length blocks and restrict sharing to within a block to enforce temporal adjacency, where semantically similar but non-adjacent (cross-block) queries are not shared. Selection Criteria Within each block, the first query serves as an initial reference and computes its critical indices across layers and heads. Following [ 49 , 42 ] and the locality bias in Observation 2 , selection budgets are allocated to three token groups: initial (sink) tokens, local tokens, and salient middle tokens. Let C sink C_{\text{sink}} and C local C_{\text{local}} denote the numbers of sink and local tokens, respectively. At decoding step t t , we obtain the middle set with a budget k k by applying the top- k k oracle over positions [ C sink , t − C local ] [C_{\text{sink}},t\!-\!C_{\text{local}}] , excluding the sink and local regions. This yields S t ∗ = { p t , i } i = 1 k S_{t}^{*}=\{p_{t,i}\}_{i=1}^{k} , where p t , i p_{t,i} is sorted and selected in descending order of attention weight. The per-head critical index set is 𝒞 t = { 1 , … , C sink } ∪ S t ∗ ∪ { t − C local + 1 , … , t } \mathcal{C}_{t}=\{1,\ldots,C_{\text{sink}}\}\cup S_{t}^{*}\cup\{t-C_{\text{local}}+1,\ldots,t\} , with a total size C = C sink + k + C local C=C_{\text{sink}}+k+C_{\text{local}} . IV-B Progressive Sliding Attention Window PSAW progressively narrows each layer’s attention window during both prefill and decoding . Consistent with Observation 2 , attention is largely localized [ 49 , 39 ] : apart from sink tokens, very early tokens receive negligible mass from later queries, and their content has already been propagated forward in lower layers. Thus, attending to them again in deeper layers is redundant. Let P ℓ ​ ( t ) P_{\ell}(t) denote the earliest visible (non-sink) position at step t t for layer ℓ \ell , and let N N be the total number of layer. We mask tokens in the index range ( C sink , P ℓ ​ ( t ) ) (C_{\text{sink}},P_{\ell}(t)) , making the visible set { 1 , … , C sink } ∪ { P ℓ ​ ( t ) , … , t } \{1,\ldots,C_{\text{sink}}\}\cup\{P_{\ell}(t),\ldots,t\} . Let ℓ s \ell_{s} be the layer depth at which pruning starts, we define P ℓ ​ ( t ) = { 0 , ℓ < ℓ s ⌊ ( − ϕ α ⋅ ℓ − ℓ s N − ℓ s ) ​ t ⌋ , ℓ ≥ ℓ s P_{\ell}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&\ell<\ell_{s}\\ \big\lfloor(1\!-\!\phi\;^{\alpha\cdot\frac{\ell-\ell_{s}}{N-\ell_{s}}})\,t\big\rfloor,&\ell\geq\ell_{s}\end{cases} (15) where ϕ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \phi\!\in\!(0,1) and α ≥ 0 \alpha\!\geq\!0 . For ℓ < ℓ s \ell\!<\!\ell_{s} , no pruning is applied to preserve early-information propagation. For ℓ ≥ ℓ s \ell\!\geq\!\ell_{s} , the boundary P ℓ ​ ( t ) P_{\ell}(t) moves monotonically forward with depth because ϕ α ⋅ ℓ − ℓ s N − ℓ s \phi^{\,\alpha\cdot\frac{\ell-\ell_{s}}{N-\ell_{s}}} decreases as ℓ \ell increases, yielding a progressively shrinking window. We adopt an exponentially decaying schedule rather than a linear one to better match attention locality biases, e.g., positional long-term decay [ 27 ] and softmax concentration, yielding tighter alignment with the empirical attention drop in long-range influence across layers (see Appendix B ). The parameter α \alpha controls the decay schedule, while ϕ α \phi^{\alpha} sets the top-layer truncation strength. A visualization of the PSAW mask is shown in Fig. 5 , where tokens in soft violet indicate masked tokens. Theoretically, by assuming attention probability mass with an exponential recency schedule beyond sink tokens, PSAW achieves a design-time certificate β th PSAW \beta_{\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{PSAW}} and a tightened MI bound that improves as ϕ α \phi^{\alpha} decreases or λ ℓ \lambda_{\ell} grows. IV-C Early Token Freezing During prefill , ETF reduces computation by freezing an expanding prefix of early tokens in deeper layers. The intuition is that information from early tokens has already been propagated forward in shallower layers; further updating them yields diminishing returns. This implementation is also supported by the cross-layer redundancy (Sec. I ) [ 15 ] . Let E ℓ ​ ( t ) E_{\ell}(t) denote the last frozen (non-sink) index at layer ℓ \ell and step t t . Tokens with positions in ( C sink , E ℓ ​ ( t ) ) (C_{\text{sink}},E_{\ell}(t)) are excluded from updates: they reuse their previous-layer hidden states, and their attention computations are skipped. Analogous to PSAW, we define E ℓ ​ ( t ) = { 0 , ℓ < ℓ s ⌊ ( − ψ γ ⋅ ℓ − ℓ s N − ℓ s ) ​ t ⌋ , ℓ ≥ ℓ s E_{\ell}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&\ell<\ell_{s}\\ \big\lfloor(1\!-\!\psi\;^{\gamma\cdot\frac{\ell-\ell_{s}}{N-\ell_{s}}})\,t\big\rfloor,&\ell\geq\ell_{s}\end{cases} (16) where ψ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \psi\!\in\!(0,1) controls the final unfrozen fraction, and γ > 0 \gamma\!>\!0 modulates the nonlinearity of the schedule. A visualization is provided in Fig. 5 , where tokens with reddish-purple edges are frozen. Aligning PSAW, giving a small, depth-decaying budget β th ETF \beta_{\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{ETF}} and a correspondingly tight MI bound, ETF achieves a design-time guarantee by increasing ℓ s \ell_{s} or μ \mu , as detailed in Appendix D . Fig. 6: Parallel CPE acceleration. Top: sequential baseline. Bottom: parallel design that fuses index manipulation with attention and directly computes TSA scoring for shared heads. ETF masking will be omitted in decoding. IV-D Parallel Acceleration Sequential execution During inference, CPE executes TSA components in the order shown in Fig. 6 (Top). After KV projection (Eq. ( 1 )), ETF freezes early tokens from further updates; during decoding, explicit ETF masking is unnecessary because only the newly generated position is updated. Next, CIS computes critical sets for shared heads using cosine gating and neighbor dilation (Eqs. ( 12 ) and ( 13 )). We then perform full scoring and build the PSAW mask for redundant-attention pruning. For heads that still require retrieval, the top- k k oracle is applied to obtain their critical sets. Finally, masks are applied so that each head attends only to its critical set. Parallel acceleration Many steps depend only on known quantities and can be prepared or executed in parallel (Fig. 6 (Bottom)). Specifically, previously computed critical sets are cached, and the PSAW mask is query-independent, allowing pre-computation. For CIS-shared heads, critical sets are already known, so full scoring is skipped and we compute attention only over valid indices (TSA scoring). Operations for shared heads and retrieval heads run concurrently, and the overall latency is determined by the slower branch.
